newsitem.title: IRAQ: Parts shortage cuts Iraq power output.
newsitem.headline: Parts shortage cuts Iraq power output.

text.p: Iraq says its power generating system is working at less than half capacity because of a lack of spare parts.

"Only 40 to 50 per cent of the capacity of the whole power generation system has been regained," Kareem Wahid Hassan, director-general of Dora power station in Baghdad, told reporters late on Wednesday night.
Hassan said Iraq had used up most of the spare parts in government stores to maintain even that low capacity.

Industry and Minerals Minister Adnan Abdul-Majeed said earlier this week over 2.5 million families in Iraq were without electricity and blamed the United States for blocking contracts on power spare parts.
Iraq's deal with the United Nations, which allows it to sell oil worth $2 billion over six months, allocates $36 million for the purchase of parts for power supply.
Hassan said that amount covered only four percent of the total needs of Iraq's power grid, and none of the money had arrived yet.
"Thirty-six million dollars is a very small amount to regain the full capacity of our power generation system," he said.
Iraq is under stringent sanctions imposed for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Hassan complained about the sluggish approval of power contracts by the U.N. sanctions committee on Iraq. He said the committee had issued purchasing orders for only three of the 68 contracts reached with foreign firms.
"Even these three which went through are not so important for maintaining power generation," he added.
Iraq's power stations were heavily bombed by U.S.-led multinational force which evicted Iraqi troops from Kuwait in 1991. Iraq said that more than 90 percent of this damage has been repaired.

Iraq needs increased electricity output to cope with rising demand from a rapidly increasing population, increasingly using household appliances, and from ambitious development plans for industry and agriculture.
"Iraq's power generation should be increased to 18,000 meqawatts by the end of 2000," he said, adding that with the current situation that target was far from being reached.
